summary: Describes MOBIKE, a mobility and multihoming extension to IKEv2 that allows the IP addresses of IKEv2 and tunnel-mode IPsec security associations to change. For example, a mobile VPN client could keep its connection to the VPN gateway while moving between networks. It is a standards-track protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: MOBIKE lets a VPN client keep its secure tunnel open when its IP address changes, for example when a laptop moves from an office network to a wireless one. It adds a few messages to IKEv2 so the client can ask the gateway to switch the tunnel to a new address without building everything again.

questions: how to keep vpn connection when ip changes
how does mobike update ipsec addresses
subtitle: Lets a VPN tunnel keep running when the client's IP address changes.

tldr.problem: In base IKEv2 the tunnel addresses of the IKE and IPsec security associations are fixed when the IKE SA is created, so a host that moves or loses an interface has to rebuild everything.
tldr.mechanism: MOBIKE adds a set of IKEv2 notifications so the party that started the IKE SA can announce extra addresses and ask the peer to switch the tunnel to a new address pair, with an optional check that the new address really works.
tldr.outcome: A mobile VPN client or a multihomed host can move between networks while keeping its existing security associations. Only one address pair is used at a time, and both ends moving at once is not supported.

facts.label: Port with MOBIKE and NAT Traversal

today: RFC 4555 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends the Internet Key Exchange protocol version 2 as defined in RFC 4306.

sections.title: Why a Tunnel Address Has to Change
sections.content:
IKEv2 authenticates two peers and sets up IPsec security associations. In the base protocol, the IKE SA and the tunnel mode IPsec SAs are created between the IP addresses in use at that moment, and those addresses become the outer, or tunnel header, addresses of the tunnel. Base IKEv2 offers no way to change them afterwards.

Addresses change in two common situations. A host that moves to a different network receives a new IP address. A multihomed host with several interfaces may want to switch to another one when the interface in use stops working.

Creating new security associations works, but it is expensive. It may need user action such as entering a code from a token card, and it involves costly calculations and several round trips. MOBIKE supplies a way to update the addresses of existing associations instead.
sections.plainLanguage: A secure tunnel is normally tied to the IP addresses it started with. MOBIKE lets the two ends update those addresses without tearing the tunnel down and setting up a new one.

sections.title: What MOBIKE Covers and Leaves Out
sections.content:
MOBIKE covers tunnel mode IPsec only. Transport mode is out of scope, as are future uses such as protecting SCTP or optimizing particular cases.

Both parties may move, but MOBIKE has no rendezvous mechanism. It cannot find addresses for the two ends at the same time, so it works best when at least one endpoint has a stable address that can be found through DNS or local configuration. Both parties may be multihomed, but only one pair of addresses is in use for an association at a time, so load balancing is out of scope.

MOBIKE also follows the IKEv2 rule that a response goes back to the address and port the request came from. That means it does not work over address pairs that offer only one-way connectivity.
sections.plainLanguage: MOBIKE only handles tunnels that carry whole packets, and it changes one address pair at a time. It does not cover load balancing, and it needs at least one end to keep a stable address.

sections.title: The Initiator Chooses the Address Pair
sections.content:
Each side may have several addresses, so there are up to N*M pairs to choose from. Some pairs do not work at all, because of incompatible IP versions, outages or problems at the local link.

MOBIKE keeps the decision simple. The party that started the IKE SA, the client in a remote access VPN, decides which pair the IPsec SAs use and works out for itself which pairs work. The other party, the gateway, only says which addresses it has and does not change any IPsec SA until the initiator asks it to. This matches how IKEv2 already works, since the initiator picks the addresses it uses when it contacts the responder.

How the initiator makes that choice is deliberately left open. MOBIKE only standardizes what is visible in the IKEv2 and IPsec messages exchanged between the peers, because that is what has to match for two implementations to work together.
sections.plainLanguage: The client that started the connection decides which address pair the tunnel uses. The gateway just lists the addresses it has and waits to be told which pair to use.

sections.title: Changing Addresses in the IPsec SAs
sections.content:
Support is signaled with a MOBIKE_SUPPORTED notification in the IKE_AUTH exchange. In the same exchange either side may list extra addresses with ADDITIONAL_IP4_ADDRESS and ADDITIONAL_IP6_ADDRESS notifications. The recipient stores them and takes no other action.

When the initiator decides to move, it updates the IKE SA with the new addresses, sets a pending update flag, updates the IPsec SAs, and sends an INFORMATIONAL request carrying UPDATE_SA_ADDRESSES from the new address. Triggers include information from lower layers, such as a new IP address or a link-down indication, and IKEv2 events such as repeated retransmissions with no valid reply. Because lower layer information can be spoofed, the RFC says to treat it as a hint and to trigger Dead Peer Detection.

The responder takes the new addresses from the IP header of the request, checks the pair against local policy, and answers UNACCEPTABLE_ADDRESSES if the pair is not acceptable. Otherwise it records the addresses, replies, optionally runs a return routability check, and then updates the IPsec SAs. The responder does not update any IPsec SA on its own, with one exception: if its current source address becomes unavailable it may switch to another one.

Address lists are replaced as a whole. There are no separate add and delete operations. The complete list is sent every time, or NO_ADDITIONAL_ADDRESSES when there are no other addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: When the client moves, it sends a short request from its new address asking the gateway to use that address. The gateway checks the request against its own rules, and if the address is acceptable it switches the tunnel over.

sections.title: Checking That the New Address Works
sections.content:
Either party can check that the other can actually receive packets at the address it claims. This return routability check SHOULD be done by default, before the IPsec SAs are updated, though it MAY be postponed or skipped where the peer is expected to behave well or where a trusted certificate already proves the address.

Any INFORMATIONAL exchange can carry the check. The sender puts unpredictable data of 8 to 64 octets into a COOKIE2 notification, and the recipient MUST copy it into the response. The original sender verifies that the value came back unchanged. If it does not match, the IKE SA MUST be closed.

When NAT Traversal is in use, NAT detection notifications can be added to ordinary INFORMATIONAL messages, such as Dead Peer Detection, to notice that a NAT mapping changed. When NAT Traversal is not enabled, every message that can update addresses must carry a NO_NATS_ALLOWED notification holding the addresses and ports the sender used. The responder compares them with the IP header and answers UNEXPECTED_NAT_DETECTED if they differ.

With several addresses on each side, Dead Peer Detection alone does not show which other path might work, so the initiator can send ordinary INFORMATIONAL requests to test a path. Because the initiator does the recovery work, the responder should use long timeouts. The RFC suggests retransmitting requests for at least five minutes before giving up.
sections.plainLanguage: Before the tunnel moves, the gateway can test that the new address really belongs to the client. It sends a value that the client must copy back exactly. If the value does not come back, the gateway does not switch.

sections.title: The New Notify Payloads
sections.content:
MOBIKE defines new IKEv2 Notify payload types. Two are error types: UNACCEPTABLE_ADDRESSES (40) and UNEXPECTED_NAT_DETECTED (41). The rest are status types numbered 16396 to 16402.

For all of them the Protocol ID and SPI Size fields are zero. MOBIKE_SUPPORTED carries empty data, which is ignored on receipt so that later versions of the protocol can use the field. The additional address notifications carry a four octet IPv4 address or a 16 octet IPv6 address. NO_NATS_ALLOWED carries the source and destination addresses and ports: 12 octets for IPv4 and 36 octets for IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: These are short labelled notes passed inside the encrypted IKE messages. Each has a number, and each says one thing: that the peer supports MOBIKE, that here is another address, or please switch now.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
MOBIKE payloads are encrypted, integrity protected and replay protected inside the IKE SA, so only the two peers can ask for an address change. The addresses in the IP header are not covered by that protection, so a NAT or an on-path attacker can change them and cause the wrong tunnel addresses to be used. The RFC limits the damage: the effect is mainly denial of service, because the traffic itself is still protected by IPsec.

Traffic redirection can also be aimed at a third party. The return routability test limits how long such an attack by an off-path attacker can last, because only a party that holds the IKE SA keys and has seen the request can answer it correctly.

Policy needs care. An association created in one place may later be used from another, so rules that depend on the peer's outer address, in particular traffic selector authorization, must account for that. Attackers may also spoof lower layer signals such as link errors to push traffic elsewhere. MOBIKE offers no protection of its own for those signals.

Finally, the address lists reveal which networks a host is attached to, and therefore something about its location. They are sent encrypted, and a peer need not disclose addresses it does not intend to use.
sections.plainLanguage: The notes themselves are locked and signed, so only the peer can ask for a switch. The addresses in the packet header are not covered by that protection, so an attacker on the path can still cause trouble, mostly by breaking the connection rather than by reading it.

items.desc: The initiator asks to move the SAs to new addresses.

items.desc: Unpredictable data for the return routability check.
